source: Let's make a cel-shading 3D game called Gallery. The core loop is paint using a simplified canvas, you're only given 45 seconds, and your canvas you can equip new colors that you've unlocked but can only have 4 available per round. The art you make gets saved and added to a new permanent portrait image in your digital gallery. You can always go up to and inspect these, by walking around in 3D in the gallery then inspecting. The most recent one you make is on a 3D easel at the front of your gallery. Every time you paint a new image with a combination of colors you haven't used before, you get to permanently unlock a new paint color you can use.

answers.ask: Cel-shading is a render style rather than a setting - should the gallery read as a clean white-cube museum, a cosy home studio, or something else?
answers.answer: Make it a clean white-cube museum rendered in cel-shaded 3D, with the easel prominently placed at the front.

answers.ask: How many finished portraits should the gallery be sized to hold before it has to expand?
answers.answer: Size the initial gallery for 12 finished portraits before it expands.

scene_prompt: Create a cel-shaded 3D game map as a clean white-cube museum gallery sized to display 12 finished portrait images. A prominent 3D easel stands at the front of the gallery holding the most recent portrait, while the remaining portrait display spaces line the surrounding white walls for players to walk up to and inspect.
blob:
## Genre
The dominant genre is Simulation because the original game centers on a repeatable painting task that produces persistent work and unlocks colors. Entertainment is secondary because the resulting gallery is also a walkable showcase.

## Shape and preset
Use `interior-single`, taken from outside Simulation’s usual shape set, because the entire playable map is one enclosed museum gallery with no exterior transition. The preset is none: no Simulation preset describes a personal painting gallery while preserving this room shape and display program.

## Config requirements
Draw `trigger-task` as a prominent cel-shaded easel and painting station at the front of the room. Use `landmark-focal` to make that easel and its newest portrait the immediate visual anchor. Create exactly 12 finished-portrait display positions in total: one on the easel and 11 evenly spaced frames on the surrounding white walls. Include a simple circulation aisle that keeps every display approachable without adding unrelated rooms or exhibits.

## Layout requirements
Place the functional `trigger-task` interaction zone at the front easel, aligned with its controls and canvas. Place exactly 12 portrait inspection markers: one at the easel and one in front of each of the 11 wall frames, offset far enough for a player to view the whole portrait. Keep the inspection positions out of the main circulation path and ensure none overlap.

## Layout components
Build one clean rectangular white-cube gallery with a clear front zone for the easel, an open central walking floor, and portrait bays along the side and rear walls. The front easel holds the newest work; 11 wall-mounted frames form a balanced perimeter sequence. Use crisp white planes, dark trim, simple ceiling lights, subtle floor reflections, and bold cel-shaded outlines. The room is fully enclosed by gallery walls. Compose the entry view directly toward the easel while letting the surrounding portrait sequence remain visible and easy to inspect.

## Render order
Use `isometric`: the clean exhibit composition and cel-shaded visual hierarchy lead, then supply the authoritative top-down.

## Scale, theme, and pipeline cost
The scale is small, driven by one room and 12 portrait positions. The theme is a clean white-cube museum in crisp cel shading. Use `P0`; one interior-only walkable surface requires no exterior-interior link or overhang capture.
